title: What should you bid for a $70 painting?
hook: The winner pays the runner-up's bid, not their own. What does that do to your best bid?

knows: you want to pay less than the item is worth to you
doesNotKnow: that when the winner pays the second-highest bid, shading your bid never helps
that inflating your bid only adds wins that lose money

misconception: Bid below your value to keep some profit, or bid above to be safe.
objective: The learner can show, against a low and a high rival bid, that in a sealed second-price auction a bid below value gives up a profitable win and a bid above value adds a losing win, so bidding true value is never worse than any other bid.

claims.text: In a sealed-bid second-price auction the highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid.
claims.source: Address: hook, predict question, stage rule line, reveal para 2. Easley & Kleinberg 2010, ch. 9 §9.4 (section unconfirmed; check against the free PDF).

claims.text: With a value of $70, a bid of $70 is never worse than any other bid, whatever the rival bids, and for some rival bids it is strictly better.
claims.source: Address: predict answer, reveal para 2 last sentence. Rule in Demo.tsx: profit = 70 - rival if bid > rival, else 0; tie goes to the rival. Node check over rival bids 0.00 to 400.00 in cents against alternative bids $0 to $200 in whole dollars: $70 is never lower than any alternative and is strictly higher for some rival bids (alternative $50: 2,000 rival values). Dominance is weak, not strict (ties); the lesson never says 'the only best'. Book argument: ch. 9 §9.4.

claims.text: At value $70 and a rival bid of $75, a bid of $90 wins, pays $75 and loses $5; a bid of $70 loses and keeps $0.
claims.source: Address: reveal para 1; stage bars at Rival $75. Arithmetic 70 - 75 = -5. Node: profit(90,75) = -5, profit(70,75) = 0.

claims.text: At value $70 and a rival bid of $60, a bid of $50 loses and earns $0, while a bid of $70 wins, pays $60 and keeps $10; the $50 bid earns less than the $70 bid against every whole-dollar rival bid from $50 to $69.
claims.source: Address: reveal para 1; stage bars at Rival $60 (the stage is pinned there at the reveal) and the sweep chart. Arithmetic 70 - 60 = 10. Node: profit(50,60) = 0, profit(70,60) = 10; over whole-dollar rival bids $0-$130, profit(50,r) < profit(70,r) exactly for r = 50..69 (20 values). v3 (2026-10-14 polish): added the sweep-range sentence. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-5): VERIFIED. Demo.tsx rule (tie to the rival): profit(50,60) = 0, profit(70,60) = 10; over whole-dollar rival bids 0-120 (the sweep chart's range), profit(50,r) < profit(70,r) exactly for r = 50..69 (20 values) and equal elsewhere. Reveal pins the stage to Rival $60, your bid $50, so the dashed (stroke-dasharray, your $50) line sits under the solid $70 line exactly as paragraph 1 says. Rival $60 and $75 are milestone-gated.

claims.text: In this lesson a tie goes to the rival (the bidder loses a tie).
claims.source: Address: stage rule line, reveal para 3. Stated rule of the model (Demo.tsx wins(): bid > rival). Not a claim about real auctions.

claims.text: A bid only decides whether you win; the price is the rival's bid, so a bid below $70 only gives up wins that pay and a bid above $70 only adds wins that lose money or break even.
claims.source: Address: reveal para 2. From the rule: a bid above 70 changes the outcome only when the rival is between 70 and the bid, where profit is negative or, at a rival bid of exactly $70, zero; a bid below 70 changes it only when the rival is between the bid and 70, where profit is positive. Same node check as c2. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-2): VERIFIED. Own case analysis with ties to the rival: a bid b > 70 differs from 70 only when 70 <= r < b, where it wins and earns 70 - r <= 0 (0 only at r = 70); a bid b < 70 differs only when b <= r < 70, where 70 wins and earns 70 - r > 0. Matches the reveal paragraph 2 and the profit() rule in Demo.tsx.

claims.text: This is why the second-price format invites honest bids.
claims.source: Address: reveal para 3. Easley & Kleinberg 2010, ch. 9 §9.4 (truthful bidding as a dominant strategy; section unconfirmed).

recall.question: In a sealed auction the winner pays the second-highest bid. An item is worth $100 to you. Which bid is never worse than any other?
options: Less than $100, to keep a margin
recall.why: Your bid only decides whether you win; the price is the rival's bid. Bidding below $100 gives up wins that pay, and above $100 adds wins that lose.
